posts.title: Flipdisc versus SOLARI
posts.summary: Two ways to build a sign out of a website, side by side.

posts.title: Live data on the board
posts.summary: Real departures, commits or a calendar - a board that flips because something actually happened.

posts.title: This blog is a board
posts.summary: The front page is a departures board, posts are trains, and reading one flips the board through it a screen at a time.
posts.body:
Every blog has an index of posts. This one has a departures board.

Each post is a train. The time column is the date it went out, the destination is the title, the platform is how many minutes it takes to read, and the remarks column tells you whether you have caught it yet: NEW in yellow until you open it, READ afterwards. Posts that are still being written sit under Arrivals with the date they are expected.

## Reading on a board

Open a post and the whole board flips into it. A post is laid out at the width of your screen and cut into pages that fit the board. Use the arrow keys, swipe, or the PREV and NEXT flaps to turn the page - every turn is the same forward-only ripple as everything else.

Switch on AUTO and the board reads itself to you: it holds each page for as long as it takes to read at an ordinary pace, then flips to the next.

## The boring, important parts

- Posts are plain Markdown files in the repository, with a title, a date, tags and a one-line summary at the top.
- Every post also has a text version: a normal web page you can read, search, copy from and share.
- There is an RSS feed, because a blog without one is just a website.

> If you want to read something properly, read the text version. If you want to watch it arrive, stay on the board.

posts.title: One canvas, fifteen hundred flaps
posts.summary: How a page that is nothing but a departures board stays smooth - and still works for a screen reader and a keyboard.
posts.body:
The board experiment asks a slightly silly question: what if a website had no text, no images and no layout - only flaps? A laptop screen holds about fifty columns and twenty-odd rows of them. That is well over a thousand cells, any of which might be flipping at once.

## Why not one element per flap

The SOLARI components draw each flap as a few nested elements with a CSS animation. That is lovely for a twelve-letter headline. For a full screen it means thousands of elements re-rendering every few frames, which is exactly how you get a page that stutters.

So the full-page board is a single canvas. Each cell is just a few numbers: the card it shows, the card it is heading for, and when its current flip began.

## Draw only what moves

Every frame, the engine walks the cells and redraws only the ones that are mid-flip. A flip is two halves: the top of the old card folding down towards the hinge, then the bottom of the new card dropping into place, each squashed toward the split line and shaded as it turns. When nothing is moving, nothing is drawn.

A full page change - every cell on screen moving - runs at a steady sixty frames per second.

## The words are still real

A canvas is a picture, and a picture is useless to a screen reader. So every page is also written out as ordinary text in the document, visually hidden, with real links you can reach with the tab key. The board is what you see; the text underneath is what the page actually says.

posts.title: Forward only
posts.summary: A split-flap cell never jumps. It steps through its drum until it lands - and that rhythm turned out to be the whole brand, and the source of its first bug.
posts.body:
On a real Solari board every character is a printed card on a drum. To go from B to A, the drum does not reverse. It turns forward through every card - C, D, E, all the way round - until A comes up again. That is the clatter you hear in a station hall.

SOLARI copies that exactly. The drum is a fixed order: a space, A to Z, 0 to 9, then punctuation. A cell only ever steps forward, one card every seventy milliseconds, with a small delay per cell so a change ripples left to right.

## The first bug

The first version of the hero cycled its messages on a plain timer: a new message every 4.2 seconds. It sounds fine. It was not.

A cell that has to travel most of the drum takes about three and a half seconds to land. With that timer, the message landed and immediately started flipping away again. On the live site the board was almost always in motion and almost never readable.

> The timer was measuring the wrong thing. It counted from when a message started, not from when you could read it.

## Hold after landing

The fix was to work out how far each cell has to travel, take the slowest one, and only start the hold once the whole board has settled. Every message now stays up for its full hold time, however far the drum had to turn to get there.

It is a small change, but it is the difference between a board that shows off and a board that tells you something.

posts.title: A website made of discs
posts.summary: Before SOLARI there was Flipdisc - a design system built on the electromechanical flip-disc sign, and the question of how far one idea can stretch.
posts.body:
The first board was not a split-flap at all. It was a flip-disc sign: a black housing, a grid of round discs, and each disc showing either its black face or its lit face - white, or fluorescent orange.

The rule was simple. Everything on the page had to look like it could hang above a bus bay. Three colours used like a sign: black is the ground, white is information, orange is the signal. If everything is orange, nothing is.

## Circles all the way down

The signature display was built from plain CSS circles driven by a five-by-seven dot font. No images, no web fonts. A board of a thousand discs was a thousand spans and one stylesheet, and it flipped column by column, fourteen milliseconds apart.

That worked beautifully for a headline. It did not work for a whole page.

## Then the whole page

The next question was obvious: could the entire site be one board? A thousand DOM elements is fine. Fifty thousand is not. So the second version, DiscField, moved the discs onto a single canvas. Unlit discs became a free CSS pattern underneath, and the canvas only drew the discs that were lit or mid-flip.

> A still page does no drawing at all.

That idea - draw only what moves - is the one that carried straight over into the board you are reading now.
